newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK base rates seen rising moderately.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK base rates seen rising moderately.

text.p: British interest rates are expected to rise moderately over the next two years as inflationary pressures remain subdued, a Reuters survey showed on Monday.

In a quarterly survey of British economic indicators, exchange and interest rates, the median of up to 27 forecasts showed bank base rates at 6.75 percent at end-1997 and at 6.50 at end-1998 from the current six percent.
By the end of first quarter 1999, base rates are expectd to have fallen below 6.5 percent.
"Growth trends are not as strong as people are making out. There are some hot spots and this is what they are concentrating on," said James McKay, UK economist at PaineWebber.
"Interest rates will have to rise but not to the scary levels people are expecting. Growth is accelerating but sterling is strong and this is an offset."
In recent days, sterling's exchange rate to the mark has strengthened to levels not seen since it fell out of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) in September 1992.
On Friday, sterling broke through 2.8000 marks, its highest level for 4-1/2 years.
A strong sterling will hold down import prices of finished goods and raw materials and retail prices, analysts say.

Forecasts from the survey, conducted between April 7 and 9, to which 32 banks, research and investment organisations contributed, reflect an increasing belief that British inflation is in a downward trend.

Forecasts from 29 economists showed on average that expectations for core retail price inflation in 1997 was 2.7 percent, while the mean of 28 RPIX forecasts for 1998 edged higher to 3.0 percent -- RPIX forecasts from Reuters surveys in January and last October gave a mean prediction of 3.0 percent for end-1997.
"Fears that inflation may rise into 1998 once the effects of a strong sterling have worn away are overstated," said Philip Shaw, UK economist at Union Plc.
"People are also worrying about average earnings growth and consumer spending - these are overstated as well."
Average earnings rose five percent in January, the highest increase since November 1992. February retail sales rose 4.4 percent year-on-year.
Forecasts for base rates ranged from six percent to 7.5 percent for end-1997 and from 5.25 percent to 8.25 percent for end-1998.
The British election on May 1 is widely expected to give the opposition Labour party a large majority over the ruling Conservatives.
McKay, who forecast base rates at 6.5 percent from third quarter 1997 to fourth quarter 1998, believes a new Labour government will adopt a tighter fiscal policy that will have a deflationary impact.
Those forecasting base rates at eight percent or above see inflation taking off with a demand-led boom, fuelled by windfall gains from flotations of building society and mutual insurance companies.
Stuart Wetherby, UK economist at Panmure Gordon, expects windfall gains to line consumer pockets with an extra 7.5 billion sterling.
"Of course they're going to spend it," he said.
He forecast base rates at 7.5 percent by end first quarter 1998 and at eight percent for the rest of 1998.
